D018-D005_h001.question:
It really started about six months ago, after the car accident on the freeway. Since then it feels like that day is stuck to me. If I hear tires screech outside the classroom or even a loud bang from kids dropping books, my whole body just locks up. Sometimes I’m suddenly right back there—I can *hear* the crunch of metal and the screaming so clearly it’s like it’s happening again, even though I know I’m standing in my classroom. It’s not random; it’s always tied to something that reminds me of the crash.

I jump at every loud sound now. If a door slams, I physically flinch, sometimes to the point the kids notice. My concentration is awful—I’ll lose my place mid-sentence while teaching or reading a simple story to the class.

I feel like I can’t really feel happy anymore, even when I’m with my husband or my students. I go through the motions, but it’s flat. I keep thinking it’s my fault, that I should’ve seen the other car, done something different. Underneath everything, I’m just…angry—at myself, at other drivers, at anyone who seems careless. It’s like this simmering rage I can’t shake.
D018-D005_h001.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h002.question:

Whenever I hear tires screech, or even just a sudden loud crash from a game I’m testing, my whole body jumps and I flinch hard. My heart races and I’m back on that highway, seeing the headlights coming at us. It’s always that night, nothing random or weird—just the crash.

Since then, I don’t really feel much joy. Even when a game I’ve worked on does well, I just feel numb. I used to like hanging out with friends, but now I’m mostly angry—at the other driver, at myself for not insisting we take an Uber. It’s like this constant simmering rage. I also keep misplacing things at work, forgetting test cases, which isn’t like me; my lead’s noticed. I’m single, live alone, and it feels like I can’t connect with people the way I used to.

A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D005_h003.question:

I jump out of my skin if someone touches my shoulder unexpectedly—my wife, a colleague, anyone. My thinking feels murky; I lose my train of thought mid-lecture, which is new for me. I used to love teaching and research, but now even good news—like a grant getting funded—barely registers. I go through the motions with my kids and my students, but I feel strangely numb.

I keep going over that day, convinced that if I’d double-checked one more safety protocol, none of it would have happened. I’m deeply ashamed I didn’t protect them better, and that feeling never really lets up.

D018-D005_h004.question:

D018-D005_h005.question:

It started about a year ago, after the accident at the old restaurant. Ever since then, it feels like my body is permanently on edge. I walk around with this constant tightness in my chest, like I’m bracing for something bad to happen. Even when service goes well, and the plates look perfect, I can’t feel proud or satisfied. I just think, “Whatever, it’s not good enough,” and move on.

The worst is when something reminds me of that night—like the smell of burning oil, a pan dropping, or hearing someone shout in the kitchen. My heart starts pounding, my hands shake, I get sweaty and dizzy. Sometimes it goes further: I don’t just remember it, I’m back there. I see the flames, hear people screaming, smell the smoke like it’s happening again. It’s so real I can’t tell it’s now; it’s like I’m watching and living it at the same time.

When that happens, I can snap. I’ve thrown pans, smashed plates, even grabbed a line cook by the collar when he came up behind me. I’m not hearing random voices or anything like that—it’s always the fire, the shouting, that night replaying itself.

I’ve been struggling a lot these past two years, ever since that car crash on the highway. At night I keep having these awful dreams where I’m back in the driver’s seat, the screeching metal, the other car spinning toward us. I wake up soaked in sweat, heart racing, convinced I’m going to die all over again.

It’s not just at night. Sometimes in the middle of the day, a horn honks outside or tires squeal and it’s like I’m suddenly *there* again. I don’t just remember it—I see it, hear it, feel it, like the scene is happening in front of me. My wife says I’ll shout or duck, but there aren’t any voices talking to me about anything else, and I don’t see or believe strange things outside of those crash moments.

I’m constantly on edge—jumpy, tense, scanning for danger. The slightest noise makes me startle. I’ve even lashed out—once I shoved my grandson when he came up behind me quietly, and I’ve slammed doors and thrown a mug when I get that rush of fear. Even when I finish a chapter of my book or get a kind review, I feel…nothing. No pride, no joy—just this dull, empty fear sitting in my chest all the time.
